instrument: Eighteen treaties negotiated by commissioners McKee, Barbour and Wozencraft
instrument_cite: none (rejected); Senate Executive Journal 1852; injunction of secrecy removed 1905-01-18
summary: The 18 treaties reserved roughly 7.4 to 7.5 million acres (sources range from about 5 to over 8.5 million). The Senate rejected all 18 in secret executive session in 1852 under pressure from the California legislature and governor, and ordered them filed under an injunction of secrecy that was lifted only on 1905-01-18.
sources_cited_by_source: Heizer 1972 citing Senate Executive Journal; NARA RG 46 and RG 75
federal_account_contrast: Royce lists the cession areas as if ceded. The nations never received the reserves, yet the land was treated as open public domain.
map_implication: Already in atlas. Add a reserve-acreage field per treaty, and show the cession polygons as 'cession never agreed (treaty rejected)', not 'ceded'.
notes: The rejection date is disputed: 1852-07-08 (Heizer, via Mechoopda) vs 1852-07-02 (NARA Prologue) vs 1852-06-28 (one web source). Later remedies: 1928 California Indians Jurisdictional Act and Court of Claims K-344 judgment (1944) with large offsets [from-memory, not verified this session]. Atlas already has these 18 rows.

source_doc: Oregon Encyclopedia, 'Willamette Valley Treaties' and 'Willamette Valley Treaty Commission'; David G. Lewis, ndnhistoryresearch.com (Tualatin 1851 post)
instrument: Treaty with the Santiam band of Kalapuya (Champoeg), Willamette Valley Treaty Commission (Gaines, Skinner, Allen)
instrument_cite: none (laid on the table in the Senate, 1852)
summary: Signed at Champoeg in spring 1851. The bands ceded most land but kept small reservations inside the Willamette Valley because they refused removal east of the Cascades. Interior Secretary Stuart opposed the treaties for not removing the Indians, and the Senate tabled them in 1852; settlers had already filed Donation Land Claims on the reserved land.
federal_account_contrast: The federal record skips straight to the ratified 1855 Kalapuya Treaty (10 Stat. 1143); the 1851 reserves inside the valley, which the bands actually agreed to, disappear.
map_implication: Add as unratified instrument; mark the 1851 proposed valley reserves as 'promised in unratified treaty, overrun by Donation Land Claims'.
notes: Sources disagree on number and dates of the Champoeg treaties (five or six) and exact signing days. Some secondary accounts say Dart recommended against ratification because the reserves were already claimed; that is partly the blogger's interpretation. Atlas lacks these.

nations: Clatsop; Lower Chinook; Wahkiakum (Waukikum); Kathlamet; Willapa; Nehalem/Tillamook bands; others
date: 1851-08-05/1851-08-09 (Tansy Point); further Dart treaties into autumn 1851
place: Tansy (Tansey) Point, near present Warrenton/Astoria, Oregon (approx. 46.18 N, 123.92 W)
instrument: Tansy Point treaties (Anson Dart, Superintendent of Indian Affairs, Oregon Territory)
instrument_cite: none; read into Senate record 1852; ICC Docket 234
summary: A set of about ten treaties let the Clatsop, Lower Chinook and neighboring bands stay in their homelands with reserved village sites and kept fishing, grazing and cranberry rights, in exchange for cessions and annuities. The Senate never ratified them. Congress paid limited compensation in 1912, and the ICC later awarded $75,000 for Clatsop and Lower Chinook land, less prior payments.
sources_cited_by_source: Chinook Nation cites the 1899 petition, 1912 appropriation, ICC award 1970
federal_account_contrast: Chinook Nation argues the 1912 payment amounted to constructive ratification; the federal government treats the treaties as void and does not recognize the Chinook Indian Nation.
map_implication: Add Tansy Point set; mark lower Columbia/Clatsop Plains as 'cession agreed only in unratified treaty; compensated later by statute/ICC'. Link to case-chinook-indian-nation-v-burgum-2026.
notes: Chinook sources give $26,308 (1912) for 762,000 acres; not checked against the 1912 act. ICC net $48,692 per Chinook sources. Atlas references Tansy Point only in cases/crosswalks, not as a treaty row.

summary: One of six treaties New Mexico Governor David Meriwether made in 1855 that set reservation boundaries and promised annuities in exchange for large cessions. notes: Commissioner of Indian Affairs report gives early June (June 10); OSU 'Oklahoma Built' catalog item 22559 dates it 1855-06-14 and labels it 'Not Ratified'. Atlas lacks.

notes: Rejection date conflict 1837-12-16 vs 1837-12-26. Acreage conflict (about 150 sq mi vs 1.5 million acres). Atlas lacks.

instrument: Treaties of Traverse des Sioux (1851-07-23) and Mendota (1851-08-05)
summary: The Senate struck Article 3 of each treaty, which defined the 20-mile-wide Minnesota River reservations, and substituted payment plus a tract to be chosen by the President. Fillmore then let them live on the struck reserve only until wanted for settlement; the 1858 treaties took the north half.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Lone Wolf the Younger'; Supreme Court Historical Society civics page and PDF of Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock; Kansas Historical Society 'Kiowa - Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock'; Encyclopedia of the Great Plains egp.law.027
place: Kiowa-Comanche-Apache Reservation, Fort Sill, Oklahoma Territory
instrument: Jerome Agreement (Cherokee Commission), 1892; Act of June 6, 1900
instrument_cite: 31 Stat. 672 (act) [from-memory, not verified this session] on page; Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903)
summary: Medicine Lodge Art. 12 required written consent of three-fourths of adult men for any cession. The Jerome Commission's signatures were alleged to be short of that (639 adult men in the 1900 census, leaving it 23 short), and obtained by misinterpretation and counterfeit signatures. Congress, after amending the terms, took about 2,991,933 acres in 1900; the Supreme Court held Congress could abrogate treaty terms unilaterally.
sources_cited_by_source: 1900 census figure via Wikipedia (citation needed tags)
federal_account_contrast: Recorded as a ratified 'agreement'; the statute Congress passed was not the agreement the signers signed, and Art. 12 consent was never met.
map_implication: Flag the 1901 KCA opening (Royce area) as 'taken without Art. 12 consent; Lone Wolf'. Atlas V022 covers this; add signature-count dispute.
notes: The 23-short figure is single-source. House passed in 1898-99, Senate defeated it Jan. 1899, then the 1900 act passed.

source_doc: Wikipedia 'Manypenny Agreement'; ABA Journal 'Aug. 15, 1876: Congress passes the Sell or Starve Act'; JURIST 2009-08-15; littlebighorn.info 'agree76' (text); Nebraska Butte County historical marker
nations: Lakota bands of the Great Sioux Reservation; Northern Arapaho; Northern Cheyenne
place: Great Sioux Reservation agencies; Black Hills (Paha Sapa)
instrument: Manypenny Agreement 1876 and Act of Feb. 28, 1877
instrument_cite: 19 Stat. 254 (1877 act); 19 Stat. 176, 192 (1876 rider) [from-memory, not verified this session]; United States v. Sioux Nation, 448 U.S. 371 (1980)
summary: The 1876 appropriations rider cut off subsistence until the Sioux gave up the Black Hills and hunting rights. The Manypenny commission then gathered signatures from about 10% of adult men, far below Fort Laramie 1868 Art. 12's three-fourths, and Congress enacted the cession in 1877.
federal_account_contrast: The 1980 Court found a taking requiring compensation but the Lakota refused payment; the atlas should not show the Black Hills as ceded.
map_implication: Render the 1877 Black Hills area as 'taken by statute; Art. 12 consent not obtained; compensation refused'.
notes: 10% figure from secondary sources (marker, advocacy). Atlas V024 covers this.

source_doc: Pres. Benjamin Harrison message on the Great Sioux Reservation, 1890 (presidency.ucsb.edu); Minot State 'A History of the Sioux Agreement' PDF; Newberry Library blog 'Standing Tall at Standing Rock'
nations: Lakota (Sicangu, Oglala, Hunkpapa, Minneconjou, Itazipco, Sihasapa, Oohenunpa); Yanktonai
instrument: Sioux Act of March 2, 1889 and Crook Commission signatures
instrument_cite: 25 Stat. 888 [from-memory, not verified this session] (one source cites 25 Stat. 1002 for the commission provision)
summary: The act broke up the Great Sioux Reservation into six reservations and opened about 9 million acres [from-memory, not verified this session], subject to three-fourths consent. Crook's commission got signatures through promises and threats, including a written promise that rations would not be cut; rations were cut soon after. Harrison certified that more than three-fourths consented.
federal_account_contrast: Federal record treats the Art. 12 threshold as met; Lakota accounts and historians describe coercion and broken promises leading to the 1890 crisis.
map_implication: Annotate 1889 cession polygons 'consent obtained under coercion; promise on rations broken'.
notes: Atlas V025 covers 1889 act.
